measures.questionText:
Pursuant to the Arizona State Constitution, Pima County seeks voter approval to
permanently adjust the expenditure base of the County as determined by the Economic
Estimates Commission. The County seeks an adjustment of $70,000,000.

voterGuide.summary:
PERMANENT BASE ADJUSTMENT
SUMMARY ANALYSIS
Pursuant to the Arizona State Constitution, Pima County seeks voter approval to permanently adjust
the expenditure base of the County as determined by the Economic Estimates Commission. If
approved by the voters, the County’s 1979-80 base expenditure limitation will be increased by
$70,000,000 adjusted each future year for population and inflation growth since 1979-80.

With voter approval, in fiscal year 2027-2028 the County’s expenditure limitation will increase by
$610,086,481, from $817,131,286 to $1,427,217,767. The County will utilize the additional
expenditure authority for any local budgetary purposes including but not limited to, public health,
safety and welfare, roads and other infrastructure.

If approved, the additional authorized expenditures will be funded from revenues obtained from state
and local sources.
voterGuide.fiscalImpact:
PERMANENT BASE ADJUSTMENT
DETAILED ANALYSIS
Pursuant to the Arizona State Constitution, Pima County, as authorized by resolution #2026-23 passed
on April 21, 2026, will seek voter approval to permanently adjust the expenditure base of the County as
determined by the Economic Estimates Commission.

With voter approval, the County will permanently increase the 1979-80 expenditure base of the County
by $70,000,000 beginning in fiscal year 2027-2028. The County will utilize the additional expenditure
authority for any local budgetary purposes including but not limited to, public health, safety and
welfare, roads and other infrastructure.

If approved, the additional expenditures authorized will be funded from revenue obtained from state
and local sources. In 2027-2028, the County’s expenditure limitation will increase by $610,086,481,
from $817,131,286 to $1,427,217,767. In Fiscal Year 2027-2028, the County only anticipates utilizing a
portion of increase in the expenditure limit. Of the $84,110,000 in projected expenditures above the
current unadjusted limit, $21,868,600 in revenue will be acquired through state sources and the
remaining $62,241,400 will be funded through existing local revenue sources. All dollar figures in this
analysis are estimates only.

In determining the revenue sources to fund the authorized additional expenditures, it is assumed that
the state and local revenues received by the County will continue to be available and increase as they
have for the past 10 years. In the past 10 years, state revenue subject to the expenditure limit has
increased by approximately 5.1% each year and local revenue has increased by approximately 3.6%
each year. If these trends hold, the County does not anticipate approaching full utilization of the
increased expenditure limit for at least 20 years.
voterGuide.passageThreshold: (6) Any political subdivision may adjust the base limit by the affirmative vote of two-thirds of the members of the governing board or by initiative, in the manner provided by law, and in either instance by approval of the proposed adjustment by a majority of the qualified electors voting at a regularly scheduled general election or at a nonpartisan election held for the nomination or election of the members of the governing board.
argumentsFor:
Vote YES on Proposition 425
Pima County’s current expenditure ceiling relies on an outdated State formula that's now 46 years old. While the
formula adjusts for general population growth and national inflation, it fails to reflect the real cost environment
counties have faced since 1980.
The costs of essential county services have grown far faster than core inflation. Heavy road and building
construction, fleet vehicle replacement, local public safety, and mandated long-term health programs have all
outpaced the state's spending limits — in every county, not just ours. The result is a structural math problem:
the County won’t even be allowed to spend revenue they already receive to keep up with these costs and
maintain current services.
Pima County isn't alone in facing this constraint. Santa Cruz County (Proposition 417) and Yuma County
(Proposition 435) are also on this ballot, each seeking a 65% increase to their base spending cap. Seven other
Arizona counties have already passed similar adjustments to maintain the autonomy they need to serve their
communities.
Proposition 425 DOES NOT raise our property taxes or tax rates. It simply allows Pima County to legally spend its
revenues so it can properly fund roads, public safety, and community needs. Vote YES on Proposition 425.

Alejandro Angel
Director of Engineering, Psomas
Tucson, AZ

Pima County's budget is throttled by a spending formula based on the year John Lennon died. That’s the year
the OG Pac-Man was released; The year Mount St. Helen’s erupted. The formula multiplies what the County
spent in the fiscal year 1979-80 by the growth in population and a predicted inflation factor that hasn't been
adjusted in nearly half a century. In 1980 a pickup truck could be purchased for $5,000. A comparable truck
today costs $40,000, but the formula still in use would assume a new vehicle cost of $20,000. The result: the
County is hindered by a threshold wildly out of step with modern costs. This problem underlies many of the
complaints citizens have with County services.
Proposition 425 updates that formula. It does not raise taxes. It does not authorize new revenue, or alter any tax
rate. It simply lets the County spend the money it already collects, within its existing budget, on services
residents already fund. Public sector services enhanced will include law enforcement, parks, animal services,
libraries, housing, health services, workforce training, and early childhood programs.
Seven of Arizona's 15 counties have made this same adjustment, including Maricopa in 1998 and Coconino and
Yavapai in 2024. Nearly every city and town in the state — Tucson, Marana, and Oro Valley among them — has
done the same. Pima County is an outlier in not having made an adjustment in the 46 years since the limit was
created.
If Prop 425 fails, the County has fewer options. It would have to rely more heavily on debt to deliver the same
services, which costs taxpayers more over time. Vote yes on Proposition 425.

Eric Robbins
Chair – Pima County Democratic Party
Tucson, AZ

As a resident of Pima County, I encourage a "YES" vote on Proposition 425. This measure represents a practical,
forward-looking step that will allow our county to better meet the evolving needs of our growing community.

Proposition 425 does not create a new tax or increase existing taxes. Instead, it modernizes an outdated
expenditure limitation formula established nearly 50 years ago that unnecessarily restricts Pima County's ability
to use its existing resources to provide essential public services.

Communities are strongest when local leaders have the flexibility to respond to today's challenges rather than
operate under rigid formulas created for a very different time. Proposition 425 gives Pima County the flexibility to
invest existing revenues where they are needed most, including public safety, parks and libraries, senior
transportation, youth programs, workforce development, and other essential community services.

Throughout Arizona, many counties, cities, towns, and public institutions have already modernized similar
expenditure limitations to better align financial policy with today's needs. These changes have provided greater
flexibility to invest in community priorities while maintaining local accountability.

Expenditure limitations promote fiscal discipline, and they should not prevent the responsible use of existing
resources to meet the evolving needs of the people. Modernizing these limitations allows public entities to
remain responsive, efficient, and accountable.

I offer this statement not in my role as Chancellor of Pima Community College, nor on behalf of the College, but
solely as a resident of Pima County who believes in responsible governance and investing in the long-term
strength of our community. For these reasons, I believe a "YES" vote on Proposition 425 is an investment in a
safer, stronger, and more prosperous Pima County.
Sincerely,

Jeffrey P. Nasse, Ph. D.

Jeffrey Nasse
Tucson, AZ

The best local government listens to residents, adapts to changing needs, and works collaboratively to solve
problems. That's the kind of leadership our communities deserve, and it's why I support Proposition 425.

For nearly five decades, Pima County has operated under a state expenditure limit written for a very different
time. Proposition 425 recognizes that communities evolve. Rather than raising taxes, it gives local leaders
greater flexibility to use existing revenue to address today's priorities while maintaining strong public
accountability. That means investing in safer roads, stronger public safety, healthier communities, parks and
public spaces, workforce opportunities, and services that support families, seniors, and neighborhoods across
Pima County.

The measure also requires continued public budgeting, audits, annual reporting, and independent oversight so
residents can have confidence that resources are being used responsibly. Communities work best when local
leaders have the tools to respond to local challenges. With seven other Arizona counties already operating
under updated expenditure limits, Prop 425 helps ensure Pima County can remain competitive while continuing
to invest in the people and places that make our region strong.

I encourage you to join me in voting YES on Proposition 425.

Miranda Schubert
Ward 6 Council Member
Tucson, AZ

Imagine trying to navigate today's world with rules and systems from almost 50 years ago. We didn’t even have
computers back then. Currently, Pima County is bound by a financial formula put in place way back in 1980.
Think about how much has changed. This outdated formula does not allow our county to use the resources it
already has to keep up with today's needs.

A yes vote for Proposition 425 will fix this and will not raise your taxes by a single cent! It will allow Pima County
to use the funds it already has.

Prop 425 will help make sure our law enforcement have the best resources, enough personnel, and competitive
pay. It will help keep our beloved parks, animal services and libraries open and accessible. It will Pima County
to keep pace with tomorrow’s needs for affordable housing, health services, workforce training, and early
childhood learning opportunities.

It’s also worth noting that we're not reinventing the wheel. Seven other Arizona counties have already updated
their formulas successfully, including Maricopa County. Even Marana, Oro Valley, and Tucson have passed
similar measures.

Ultimately, voting 'yes' on Proposition 425 is about being smart and forward thinking. It’s about giving our county
the tools it needs to best serve us, without costing us more. It’s about building a stronger, more vibrant Pima
County for everyone, today and tomorrow.

Sylvia Lee
Former Pima County Supervisor, District 3 & Former Governing Board Chair, Pima Community College
Tucson, AZ

As a long-time community organizer and now Chair of the Pima County Board of Supervisors, I've learned that
lasting progress comes when local communities have access to the tools they need to solve local challenges.
That's why I support Proposition 425.

When local communities identify a need, they should have the ability to act. But today, Pima County is still
constrained by a state spending formula written nearly five decades ago. Proposition 425 updates that outdated
law so the county can use revenue it already has to invest in the priorities our communities have today— all
without raising taxes.

Those priorities look different across the rural, urban, suburban, border, and other communities in Pima County,
but they all matter. Safe roads and streetlights. Parks and libraries. Public health services. Responsive public
safety. Programs that help seniors remain independent, prepare workers for good-paying jobs, and give children
opportunities to succeed.

Good government also requires public trust. That's why Proposition 425 includes ongoing public budgeting,
independent audits, annual reporting, and citizen oversight to ensure transparency and accountability.

The challenges facing Pima County today are not the same as they were nearly 50 years ago, and our
communities deserve the flexibility to respond to them. Seven other Arizona counties—including Maricopa—
have already updated their expenditure limits, and it's time we do the same.

Proposition 425 is a practical, responsible update that keeps decision-making closer to the people it affects
most.

I hope you'll join me in voting YES on Proposition 425.

Jen Allen
Chair and District 3 Supervisor, Pima County Board of Supervisors
Tucson, AZ

As Vice Mayor of Tucson and Council Member for Ward 1, I've spent my time on the Council fighting for what our
community needs to thrive: safe streets, strong public services, and a local government that works for the
people.

That's why I support Proposition 425.

Nearly five decades ago, Pima County's expenditure-limit formula was set. Our region has grown a lot since
then, but that formula hasn't. It's kept the county from fully investing the resources it already has, which means
dollars meant for Tucson and Pima residents too often get left on the table instead of going to work in our
neighborhoods.

Proposition 425 fixes that. It's a common-sense update that creates zero new taxes. It simply allows Pima
County to invest the revenue it already collects in the services that keep our communities strong.

For Tucson residents, that means real, everyday investments: well-maintained roads and bridges, parks and
public spaces our families can enjoy, public safety and public health, and essential programs like senior
transportation, Meals on Wheels, workforce training, and after-school care. I've always believed in investing in
ourselves and making sure our local government has every tool it needs to meet community needs, and Prop
425 does exactly that.

This measure also builds in ongoing public budgeting, audits, reporting, and independent oversight, so
residents can trust these dollars are spent responsibly and transparently.

Seven other Arizona counties, including Maricopa, have already modernized their expenditure limits. It's time
Pima County has that same ability to serve its residents, without an outdated formula standing in the way.

I encourage you to join me in voting YES on Proposition 425.

Lane R. Santa Cruz
Vice Mayor
Tucson, AZ

VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 425: PROTECT PIMA COUNTY'S $2.9 BILLION TOURISM ECONOMY
Pima County's tourism industry generated $2.9 billion in direct travel spending in 2024, representing nearly 12%
of Arizona's total tourism revenue and supporting thousands of local jobs. This economic engine depends on
infrastructure that works.
Proposition 425 addresses a critical problem: Pima County's spending authority remains tied to a 1979-80
baseline, when tourism looked vastly different. Today's 7+ million annual visitors traveling to Saguaro National
Park, Reid Park Zoo, and Tucson's cultural attractions need modern roads, maintained infrastructure, and

responsive public services. Outdated spending limits prevent necessary investments that keep visitors safe and
satisfied. Quality infrastructure directly impacts tourism competitiveness. When roads are well-maintained,
visitors travel easily between attractions. When public safety resources are adequate, tourists feel secure
exploring our region. When County services function efficiently, the overall visitor experience improves, leading
to positive reviews, return visits, and recommendations that drive future tourism growth.
Without this adjustment, Pima County cannot adequately fund the infrastructure and services our tourism
economy requires. Competing destinations invest in their visitor infrastructure; we risk falling behind.
Critically, Proposition 425 uses existing state and local revenue sources—no new taxes. It simply allows the
county to spend revenue it already receives. With nearly $3 billion in annual tourism spending and 920 million in
travel industry earnings at stake, we cannot afford infrastructure deterioration.
Vote YES on Proposition 425. Invest in infrastructure. Protect tourism jobs. Keep Pima County competitive.
J. Felipe Garcia, President & CEO, Visit Tucson

Jose Garcia
President & CEO
Tucson, AZ


Heather Molina
EVP
Tucson, AZ

As an elected official in the City of Tucson and a resident of Pima County I ask you to join me in supporting
Proposition 425.

Proposition 425 will update an outdated State spending formula by allowing Pima County to make better use of
the revenue it already has instead of relying on tax increases. Similar updates have occurred in seven Arizona
counties – including Maricopa. Pima County deserves the same opportunity.

The measure includes public budgeting, independent audits, annual reporting, and citizen oversight to ensure
transparency and accountability.

If you support your local government having the flexibility to make better use of the revenues they already have, I
encourage you to vote YES on Proposition 425.

Kevin Dahl
City of Tucson Council Member
Tucson, AZ

Prop 425 will update an outdated formula from 1980 that prevents Pima County from being able to use its full
resources to provide services for county residents. The formula was created 46 years ago before 4 decades of
large-scale population growth, aging roads, and bridges, and increasing demands placed on law enforcement
and community services. This measure will not increase the tax rate, and a vote against raising the expenditure
limit will not lower taxes, either. However, a vote against the measure will hamper Pima County’s ability to meet
the growing needs of our community.
At its core, Proposition 425 is about common-sense fiscal management. Pima County is consistently lauded for
a commitment to sound financial priorities and a strong relationship with the private sector such as:

• Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in Financial Reporting from the Government Finance Officers
Association for the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report. Pima County has received the GFOA Award 25
consecutive years.
• Consistent AA to AAA bond ratings.
• A multi-year economic development collaboration with The Chamber of Southern Arizona intended to drive
business attraction, workforce training, and international investment. Finally, the measure includes built-in
accountability. County expenditures will continue to be publicly budgeted and audited, with annual reporting to
the Arizona Auditor General regarding the expenditure limit. The Board proactively created the Debt and
Financial Transparency Commission to provide transparency and accountability to support, for now and into the
future, “responsible fiscal stewardship” of County debt, use of our tax dollars, and the County’s financial
decisions.
It is important to support this measure and allow Pima County to increase its expenditure limitation formula to
ensure our county can effectively manage its resources and continue to thrive and be a great community
partner throughout the region.

Danette Bewley
President/CEO
Tucson Airport Authority

Danette Bewley
President & CEO
Marana, AZ

I had the honor of serving our country in the United States Air Force, later serving students and families on the
Sahuarita Unified School District Governing Board, and today I have the privilege of serving the residents of
Sahuarita as Mayor. Strong communities don't happen by accident. They are built through thoughtful planning,
responsible leadership, and investments that create opportunity for current residents and future generations.
That's why I support Proposition 425. The state expenditure-limit formula that governs Pima County was created
more than 46 years ago. Since then, our communities have grown, our economy has evolved, and the demands
on infrastructure, public safety, public health, and essential community services have changed dramatically.
Yet Pima County is still operating under that outdated formula. While I’m ardently opposed to the County’s
recent decision to increase property taxes, I acknowledge that Proposition 425 is a practical solution that does
not raise or lower property taxes. It simply updates the formula so Pima County can use available revenues to
invest in the services that support thriving communities —from maintaining roads and bridges to strengthening
public safety, supporting workforce training, and preserving parks, libraries, senior services, and other programs
that improve quality of life. As mayor, I've seen how strong communities attract businesses, support families,
and create opportunities. That's why economic development and quality of life go hand in hand. Prop 425 helps
ensure Pima County can remain competitive with the seven other Arizona counties — including Maricopa —
that have already modernized their expenditure limits. It’s a win-win. We can support the health and safety of
residents and families and make our communities more prosperous without any added burden on taxpayers. I
encourage you to join me in voting YES on Proposition 425 on November 3.

Tom Murphy
Mayor
Sahuarita, AZ

To be honest, we flipped a coin, and we’re apparently supporting Proposition 425. The Board of Supervisors
made the easy decision to ask voters to approve a Permanent Base Adjustment adding $70 million to the
county’s 1979-80 base. And, as it should be, voters will ultimately decide whether to approve it.
It is not a tax increase, a bond measure or authorization to immediately spend another $610 million. It would
simply allow the county to spend the money it collects without relying on increasingly creative accounting and
taking on debt. But with great power comes great responsibility — specifically, financial discipline by our
elected officials.
And since it took 46 years for the county to ask voters to increase the limit, that discipline isn’t just limited to the
four Democrats and one Republican currently in office. Their successors also need to use taxpayer dollars
wisely. And we at the Tucson Agenda will be there, digging through proposed budgets, adopted budgets,
supplemental budgets and, yes, as many audits as we can get our hands on.
“Trust, but verify” is an old Russian proverb, but it’s especially apt for the Fourth Estate’s role in covering how
Pima County spends public money.

Joe Ferguson
Senior Reporter, Tucson Agenda
Tucson, AZ

Serving as the Mayor of Tucson, I have a strong commitment to strengthening our infrastructure, supporting
working families, growing our economy, and building a resilient city where everyone has the opportunity to
thrive.

We all need safe roads, reliable public services, healthy neighborhoods, quality parks, safe public spaces, and
opportunities for young people and working families to succeed. Local government should have the ability to
invest in those priorities. Instead, Pima County is still constrained by a state expenditure-limit formula created
nearly fifty years ago.

Proposition 425 updates that outdated law so that Pima County can use the revenue it already has to invest in
the services residents depend on. Importantly, this can be done without raising taxes by a single penny.

Pima County invests in public health and public safety, maintaining roads and bridges, sustaining parks and
libraries, and continuing programs like youth workforce development, senior transportation, Meals on Wheels,
and workforce training. These programs strengthen our neighborhoods and communities, expand economic
opportunity, and improve quality of life for everyone.

Proposition 425 also includes strong public accountability. Pima County expenditures will continue to be
budgeted, audited, and reported publicly, with an independent oversight committee providing additional
transparency.

Seven other Arizona counties, including Maricopa, have already modernized their expenditure limits. Pima
County deserves the same flexibility to invest in its residents and respond to today’s challenges with today’s
resources. Our residents deserve to be the beneficiaries of the resources we generate.

Please join me in voting YES on Proposition 425.

Regina Romero
Tucson Mayor
Tucson, AZ

Strong neighborhoods start with investing in people. That means creating opportunities for our youth,
supporting working families, maintaining safe streets and parks, and making sure every neighborhood has the
resources it needs to thrive no matter the ZIP Code.

That's why I am voting YES on Proposition 425.

Every community has different priorities, but they all deserve the opportunity to succeed. Proposition 425 gives
Pima County the flexibility to invest existing revenue where it's needed most—whether that's maintaining
infrastructure, strengthening public safety, supporting public health, improving parks and public spaces, or
continuing programs that help families, seniors, and our local workforce.

This measure does not create a new tax or raises taxes. It simply updates an outdated state law that has limited
Pima County's ability to fully use the resources already available to serve residents.

Proposition 425 also includes strong accountability measures, including public budgeting, independent audits,
annual reporting, and public oversight, so residents can continue to see how their tax dollars are being spent.

When we invest in our neighborhoods, we invest in our future. Proposition 425 gives Pima County the flexibility
to meet today's needs while planning for tomorrow.

I hope you will join me in voting YES on Proposition 425.

Selina Barajas
Ward 5 City Council Member
Tucson, AZ

As a lifelong Southern Arizonan—and as someone who has served our community on the Tucson Unified School
District Governing Board, the Pima County Board of Supervisors, and now in Congress—I know how deeply
residents depend on strong, responsive local government.

That is why I support Proposition 425.
Pima County is still operating under an expenditure-limit formula established in 1980. In the 46 years since, our
population has grown, roads and public facilities have aged, and the demands placed on public health and
essential community services have changed dramatically.

Proposition 425 does not increase the tax rate. Instead, it will update the formula used to determine how much
of its available revenue Pima County can spend to serve residents.

Passing this measure will help us maintain the critical infrastructure our families need, like roads and bridges,
and it will help keep open our parks, pools, and libraries, senior transportation, Meals on Wheels, after-school
programs, as well as workforce training and apprenticeships.

These services are not luxuries. They help residents remain healthy and independent, prepare workers for good-
paying jobs, support families, and make communities attractive to employers and investment.

Seven other Arizona counties—including Maricopa—have already passed similar adjustments, giving them a
competitive advantage. We need to pass Prop 425 in order to create a level playing field for Pima County
residents, preserve a high quality of life, and strengthen our economy.

This measure will give Pima County the tools to plan responsibly, address problems before they become more
expensive, and continue delivering the services our communities rely upon.

Please join me in voting YES on Proposition 425 by November 3.

Adelita Grijalva
Congresswoman
Tucson, AZ

The Tohono O’odham Nation and Pima County continue to be partners and allies on several initiatives designed
to support housing, health and public safety. My Vice Chairwoman Johnson, myself, and my administration
support Proposition 425 because of these shared priorities.

For years, politicians at the state level have cut, taken, or redirected funding that is intended to be used for local
public services. This measure will provide Pima County with a locally controlled funding source. Seven other
counties—including Maricopa—have already passed a similar fix, giving them a competitive advantage. We
need to pass this measure to keep Pima County on a level playing field with the people of other counties, both in
their quality of life and in strengthening our local economy.

Proposition 425 empowers Southern Arizonans to continue to support each other and our region. I respectfully
request your support for Prop. 425. Together we are stronger.

Verlon M. Jose, Chairman of the Tohono O’odham Nation

Verlon Jose
Chairman
Sells, AZ
argumentsAgainst:
Pima County Proposition 425 is being presented as a “no new taxes” measure. In truth, it seeks to lift the current
cap on county spending—a limit that exists because the county is approaching the maximum it is legally
permitted to spend from local revenues despite strong collections.

This raises a more fundamental question: Why not prioritize returning surplus funds or excess growth to
taxpayers through meaningful tax reductions? Escalating property taxes are placing an unsustainable burden on
residents, particularly longtime homeowners at risk of being priced out of their homes.

Of particular concern is that approving the measure would significantly expand the Board of Supervisors’
spending authority. What officials describe as a modest adjustment to the spending limit (potentially raising the
base substantially) could open the door to higher future expenditures—and, by extension, pressure for tax
increases—without additional voter approval on the cap itself.

Voters must weigh whether expanding the county’s spending authority is truly necessary when revenues are
already robust. Instead of approving mechanisms that risk higher taxes down the road, residents should insist
that county officials exercise fiscal restraint and prioritize efficiency or rate reductions. This approach would
deliver direct relief to taxpayers and help restore affordability in our communities.

Government must live within its means—not continually expand those means at the expense of the people it
serves. I urge Pima County voters to carefully consider these implications before casting their ballots.

Janet Wittenbraker
Tucson, AZ

Dear Pima County Voters;

Vote NO on Prop 425. Pima County already imposes one of the highest effective property tax rates among
Arizona’s 15 counties, with combined average rates at or near the top. Despite this heavy burden on residents,
the current County administration admits it collects more tax revenue than it is currently authorized to spend.

Rather than providing relief by lowering rates, county leaders are asking voters to raise the spending limit. A
“yes” vote on Prop 425 would let just three County Supervisors approve up to half a billion dollars in additional
spending.

This is the wrong choice at the wrong time. Pima families are already squeezed by housing affordability
challenges, inflation, and rising costs. Increasing the County’s authority to spend more of your money will not
improve affordability or efficiency—it will simply enable further expansion of government spending.

We don’t need higher spending authority. We need better financial management and fiscal restraint. Let’s get rid
of the waste, fraud and abuse of our tax dollars. Let’s reject excessive spending. Vote NO on Prop 425.

Gary Olson and Nancy Harris
Long time voters,
Tucson, AZ

Gary Olson
Active Voter
Tucson, AZ

Nancy Harris
Active Voter
Tucson, AZ

Debt service and bond proceeds are largely exempt from Arizona’s constitutional expenditure limit. That means
the spending limit does not directly stop the County from borrowing. What it does constrain is the overall size
and growth of government operations.
When voters permanently raise that limit by hundreds of millions of dollars, the political and fiscal pressure to
stay disciplined drops. Larger operating capacity often leads to larger capital wish lists, which are frequently
financed with new debt rather than cash. Those bonds become fixed, multi-year claims on the same property-
tax base that funds schools, libraries, flood control, and the rest of local government.
You already help service the County’s existing debt through your property taxes. Do not hand the Board a
permanent expansion of spending power that makes it easier to add even more long-term obligations for you
and your children to repay. Vote NO on Proposition 425.

Mohit Asnani
Tucson, AZ

Vote NO on Prop 425! Aren’t you tired of being manipulated and misled? Well, take a better look at Prop 425.
Voters approved a ballot measure in 1980 that put a spending limit on the runaway spending of the County. The
limit for 1979-80 was established at $93 million, and was to increase yearly based on inflation and population
growth. By now, that limit has increased to $817 million!! But the County doesn’t think that’s enough.

The County is proposing Prop 425 which is described as a permanent increase of $70 million to the 1979-80
expenditure base. Now, $70 million more doesn’t sound that outrageous, does it? Oh, but wait! This is not $70
million added to TODAY’S limit; this is $70 million added to the 1979-80 base limit, which, with inflation and
population growth will have increased to $610 million! The County is asking us to approve adding $610 million
MORE to the present $817 million spending limit. This is an increase of 75%, and the spending limit for the
County, almost overnight, goes from the present $817 million to almost $1.5 BILLION! And this is a permanent
change which will continue to increase by inflation and population growth PERMANENTLY!

This is insane! And when the County has the authority to spend this amount of money, they will claim they need
to, and we will see all our taxes go through the roof. You think our sales taxes and property taxes are too high?
Just wait.

Dr. Sherrylyn Young
Tucson, AZ

I’m a lawyer who has lived here for 60+ years, and represented Arizona cities, counties and other political
subdivisions as part of my practice over several decades. I oppose Proposition 425.

This measure permits a drastic 75% increase of over $610 Million in spending authority, almost immediately,
and should be honestly presented as such. Operative words on the ballot have instead been crafted to make it

seem like the County is “only” asking for a $70 Million “adjustment.” They’re really asking permission to spend
$610 Million beyond the current limit for the next fiscal year! And thereafter, Prop 425 authorizes increased
spending by 75% FOREVER.

Under Article IX of the Arizona Constitution, expenditure limits can be adjusted for specific periods to meet
emergencies, and are automatically adjusted every year to account for population increases and inflation. Our
county wants a perpetual increase far greater than those factors can justify.

It’s true that increasing the expenditure limit, by itself, doesn’t directly increase taxes. It’s a back door, however,
to requiring future tax increases. When the County spends more, they inevitably must increase their revenue,
and that means increasing taxes.

We are told that the County “doesn’t anticipate” spending as much as this “adjustment” would allow . . . well,

• force our elected officials to be accountable to The People of Pima County.

Voting for proposition 425 will give the county permission to spend hundreds of millions of unrestricted dollars,
every year, for any purpose it chooses without the consent of the community it serve.

The choice is clear...

VOTE NO ON PROPOSITION 425!!!


Jay Tolkoff
Tucson, AZ

Vote NO on the proposed Pima County Permanent Base Adjustment! County government is simply not
responsible enough to warrant receiving a permanent increase in the base adjustment. Giving the county more
money will only enable them to spend additional funds on pet projects that do not serve the majority of the
community. The county is simply not a responsible party able to manage millions of dollars of taxpayer funds--
just look at the state audits year after year. Taxpayers are asked each year to open their wallets and give more
and more money to the county. Each year the county budget increases going from $1.2 billion to almost $2
billion dollars in less than a ten-year span. Unfortunately, taxpayer earning capacity has not increased at the
same rate. The result is that taxpayers will simply be asked to give more and more funding while they struggle to
provide for their families and households on limited income. The Pima County taxpayers deserve better
accountability for the funds they have already provided to the county. Pima County taxpayers do not need to be
straddled with a long term permanent base adjustment that will be harmful to elderly on limited incomes,
working families who cannot afford increases in property taxes, and individuals who live paycheck-to-paycheck,
among others. Be responsible and vote "NO" on increasing the base expenditure limit.

Dr. JoAnn di Filippo, PhD
Tucson, AZ

Vote NO on Pima County Proposition 425.

Proposition 425 permanently raises the county’s 1979-80 spending base by $70 million. That single change
explodes the annual expenditure limit by roughly $610 million—from about $817 million to $1.43 billion starting
in FY 2028. Officials openly say they won’t need that much room for at least 20 years. So why lock in a 75%
permanent increase now? Arizona voters created the expenditure limit in 1980 for a reason: to force government
to prioritize and live within reasonable bounds that grow only with population and inflation. Once the higher
ceiling is set, it becomes the new normal. Spending almost always expands to fill available capacity. Future
Boards of Supervisors gain far more room to launch big projects or grow programs without returning to the
voters.
A NO vote does not cut existing services or raise (or lower) your taxes. It simply keeps the current limit in place.
If genuine needs arise, the county can seek a temporary override or a smaller, better-justified adjustment later.
Permanent blank-check authority is the opposite of accountability. Don’t hand over decades of spending power
in one vote. Demand prioritization and efficiency first. Vote NO on Proposition 425.

Eileen Wilson
President - United Republicans for Arizona
Green Valley, AZ

measureRecords.whatItDoes:
Pursuant to the Arizona State Constitution, Pima County seeks voter approval to permanently
adjust the expenditure base of the County as determined by the Economic Estimates Commission.
If approved by the voters, the County’s 1979-80 base expenditure limitation will be increased by
$70,000,000 adjusted each future year for population and inflation growth since 1979-80.
measureRecords.yesMeans:
A “YES” vote shall have the effect of allowing Pima County to adjust its 1979-80 base
expenditure limit.
measureRecords.noMeans:
A “NO” vote shall have the effect of not allowing Pima County to adjust its 1979-80 base
expenditure limit.

With voter approval, in fiscal year 2027-2028 the County’s expenditure limitation will increase by
$610,086,481, from $817,131,286 to $1,427,217,767. The County will utilize the additional
expenditure authority for any local budgetary purposes including but not limited to, public health,
